findings.issue_text: [BUG] The new file imports AdminPermissionManagement.TOKEN_EXCHANGE statically but never uses it, so Keycloak's checkstyle UnusedImports rule fails the build. Any CI or local build running the project checkstyle profile (default for this repo) fails on 'UnusedImports - import static ...AdminPermissionManagement.TOKEN_EXCHANGE' before tests even compile.

[BUG] The onEvent handler now calls Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) but the diff adds no import of org.keycloak.common.Profile to AdminPermissions.java, which previously did not reference Profile. Compilation of services fails with 'cannot find symbol: Profile' unless the class already imported it before this change; the diff shows no import hunk, so the file does not compile as written.

[ADVISORY] The diff replaces the blank line after the class declaration with a line containing trailing whitespace ('+    '). Keycloak's checkstyle RegexpSingleline 'trailing spaces' check fails the build; trivial to fix but it blocks merge until corrected.

[ADVISORY] The private method getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken) added in this diff has no caller anywhere in the class or the diff. Dead code: the next reader must reason about an evaluation-context path (ClientModelIdentity/DefaultEvaluationContext with kc.client.id attribute) that is never exercised, and it silently rots if the token-exchange V2 design it was copied from changes; it should be deleted until a caller exists.

[BUG] The ClientRemovedEvent handler calls clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false), which under the V2 evaluator (MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() returns ClientPermissionsV2) is implemented as `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`, so any client deletion while ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled throws from inside the provider event listener. With the feature enabled, every admin client-delete (and identically role-delete/group-delete via the same listener pattern) blows up with an unexpected UnsupportedOperationException/500 instead of completing the removal — the very scenario the listener exists to clean up. The new feature gate does not prevent this; it only skips the handler when the feature is off, and V2 is active precisely when the feature is on.

[ADVISORY] Wrapping all three removal events (role, client, group) in `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` disables the legacy V1 cleanup path (setPermissionsEnabled(false) on removal) whenever the feature flag is off, even for realms using the non-V2 fine-grained permission toggles. Operators who disable the feature after having used fine-grained permissions (or deployments where V1 permissions are active without the preview flag) leave orphaned permission resources/policies behind when clients, roles, or groups are deleted, silently accumulating stale authorization rows that reappear if the feature is re-enabled.

[ADVISORY] The MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE scope is added to the schema and wired into canMapClientScopeRoles(), but no test in this diff exercises it — PermissionClientTest covers MAP_ROLES and MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE (testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient) and never the client-scope map-roles path. A regression in canMapClientScopeRoles or the MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE scope registration (e.g. a typo in the constant, or scope never granted during evaluation) ships undetected; the first signal is a user with granted client-scope role-mapping permission getting ForbiddenException in production.

[ADVISORY] The private method getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken) is dead code — nothing in the class invokes it because canExchangeTo and all exchange-related methods throw UnsupportedOperationException. Next change to token-exchange support in V2 must first determine whether this half-attached evaluation context (with its kc.client.id attribute) is the intended entry point or a leftover from a reverted approach; until then it rots invisibly and misleads readers into thinking token-exchange evaluation is partially wired.

[ADVISORY] In getClientsWithPermission, `granted.add(resource.getName())` returns the resource name, which getOrCreateResource sets via resolveClient() to `client.getId()` (the internal UUID), while callers consuming this set to filter the clients list match against client representations whose `id` field is the internal id but whose user-facing identifier is `clientId`. If any caller filters by clientId rather than internal id (the natural mistake given the method name and the admin REST surface), the filtered list silently drops every granted client; the existing tests only assert non-empty/empty results, not the identity of the returned strings, so a name-vs-id mismatch passes the suite.

[ADVISORY] The new javadoc on requireView() (and requireListClientScopes()-adjacent void require methods) states 'Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}' for methods declared `void` that throw ForbiddenException — the contract is documented as a boolean query when it is an enforcement call. Call-site authors reading the interface contract treat requireView() as a check they can call speculatively, and get an HTTP-500-style ForbiddenException propagated instead of a false return, producing wrong exception handling in new admin endpoints.

[BUG] The PR wraps the pre-existing role/client/group removal cleanup logic in Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ), changing behavior that is not traceable to the stated intent of adding a Clients resource type. In deployments where the feature was previously compiled-in but this listener previously ran unconditionally, disabling the feature now silently skips setPermissionsEnabled(false) cleanup on role/client/group deletion, leaving orphaned permission resources in the database that the old code removed — a data-hygiene regression unrelated to adding the Clients resource type.

[BUG] ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, but the AdminPermissions event listener added in this same diff calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false) on every ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled. With the V2 permissions path active, deleting any client throws UnsupportedOperationException during event handling, turning client deletion (a previously working operation, now also exercised by testManageAllClients' delete step) into a 500 error instead of completing the removal.

[ADVISORY] getEvaluationContext and the TOKEN_EXCHANGE static import are dead code in this diff — getEvaluationContext is never called (all token-exchange methods throw UnsupportedOperationException) and TOKEN_EXCHANGE is referenced nowhere in the class body. Future readers must reason about an evaluation-context path that cannot execute; the next change to token-exchange support risks building on a code path that has never been exercised, and the unused import fails strict import checks.

[ADVISORY] The MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE scope is added to the schema and canMapClientScopeRoles is implemented, but no test in this diff exercises it and no admin REST path in the diff is shown enforcing it, unlike MAP_ROLES and MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE which testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient covers. A regression in the map-roles-client-scope evaluation (e.g., a wrong scope constant or a mis-wired caller) ships undetected; operators granting the scope get behavior that is never validated, breaking the parity-with-V1 invariant the other five scopes' tests establish.

[ADVISORY] Twelve overridden methods throw UnsupportedOperationException rather than the interface being narrowed or the V2-only surface being split out, so any caller not updated in this diff that touches exchangeTo, resource(), getPermissions, etc. fails at runtime instead of at compile time. Any existing or out-of-tree caller of ClientPermissionEvaluator's per-client policy-management methods (e.g., the admin PermissionsResource endpoints) that reaches the V2 implementation gets a raw UnsupportedOperationException/500 instead of a documented 4xx; the compiler can no longer flag new call sites added later.

[BUG] Under the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature flag the removal listener calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(...), which in the V2 implementation (ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled) throws UnsupportedOperationException, so deleting a client while the feature is enabled fails instead of cleaning up permissions. Client deletion (and role/group deletion via the same guarded block) raises UnsupportedOperationException during the removal event, breaking a core admin operation for realms that enabled the feature; if the flag gates V1 management() the entire block now dead-codes for realms without the feature, leaving orphaned permission resources on removal.

[BUG] resolveClient accepts either the internal UUID or the clientId and returns the canonical id, but the resource is created/stored named by whatever string the permission-creation path passed, while ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission looks the resource up by client.getId() — the two paths can disagree on the resource name for the same client. A permission created referencing the client by clientId produces a resource named by the clientId; a subsequent evaluation for that client does findByName(server, client.getId()) and misses it, so the granted permission silently does not apply (deny instead of allow), or two resources accumulate for one client and list/getClientsWithPermission reports inconsistent results depending on which name was used.

[BUG] getClientsWithPermission iterates every resource of type Clients and calls hasGrantedPermission, which invokes root.evaluatePermission (a full policy evaluation, loading policies from the store) once per client resource — an N+1 evaluation loop over a collection that scales with the number of clients in the realm. On any admin client-listing path that filters by granted permission, a realm with thousands of clients performs thousands of full permission evaluations per request, turning the list endpoint into an O(n) policy-evaluation workload with no pagination or batching; large realms see severe latency and DB load on a hot admin path.

[ADVISORY] getEvaluationContext (and the TOKEN_EXCHANGE static import it supports) is dead code — nothing in the class calls it, and canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException. The next maintainer must reason about and possibly maintain an evaluation-context path that is never exercised; when token-exchange support is added it will likely be copied from this stale skeleton rather than the real V1 behavior.

[ADVISORY] The evaluate-permissions-and-scan-for-scope loop is duplicated three times (hasPermission(ClientModel,String), hasPermission(String), hasGrantedPermission), differing only in how the Resource is obtained. When the scope-matching logic changes (e.g. to support scope collections or wildcard grants), three copies must be updated in lockstep; missing one yields evaluator methods that disagree on whether a scope is granted — a silent authorization inconsistency.

[ADVISORY] canMapRoles/canMapCompositeRoles/canMapClientScopeRoles in V2 drop the previous base-class fallback entirely and rely solely on hasPermission, while canConfigure and canManage keep the admin-role short-circuit — an inconsistent ownership of 'who can map roles' between the role-based and FGAP paths. An admin holding MANAGE_CLIENTS but no explicit map-roles permission can manage the client yet cannot map its roles in V2, a behavior change vs V1 that any caller (or test) assuming role-superset semantics will hit as an unexpected ForbiddenException.

[ADVISORY] getPermissionsResource, getScopePermissionsResource, and createPermission were converted from instance methods to static methods taking ManagedClient, a breaking signature change to a shared test base class whose out-of-tree subclasses call the no-arg forms. Any external test module extending AbstractPermissionTest and calling getPermissionsResource() with no arguments no longer compiles after upgrading, with no deprecation window.

[BUG] The RoleRemovedEvent/ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent cleanup handlers were silently re-gated behind Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ), changing previously unconditional cleanup behavior as an incidental side effect of a PR whose stated intent is only to add a Clients resource type. When the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature is disabled (the pre-existing V1 fine-grained permissions deployments), deleting a role, client, or group no longer calls setPermissionsEnabled(..., false), leaving orphaned permission resources and policies in the database that reappear/grant stale access if the feature is later re-enabled.

[BUG] ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, but the ClientRemovedEvent handler in AdminPermissions.management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false) is the code path that must run on every client deletion, so V2 realms throw during client removal. With the feature enabled and MgmtPermissionsV2 in use, deleting any client propagates an UnsupportedOperationException out of the event listener instead of disabling its permissions, failing the client-deletion flow that the intent of the PR (managing client permissions) presupposes works.

[BUG] The ClientRemovedEvent/RoleRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent handlers call clients().setPermissionsEnabled(...) which now throws UnsupportedOperationException when the V2 ClientPermissions implementation is active under the enabled ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature, so deleting a client/role/group in a V2 realm blows up inside event processing. When the feature is enabled and the V2 permission implementation is in use, entity deletion triggers UnsupportedOperationException from the event listener (instead of the previous no-op/cleanup), failing or polluting the delete path for clients, roles, and groups.

[ADVISORY] Wrapping the removal-event cleanup in Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) means authorization resource cleanup for deleted clients/roles/groups no longer runs when the feature is off, leaving orphaned permission resources in the database. An operator who disables the feature after having created fine-grained permissions accumulates stale resources; re-enabling the feature later resurrects permission entries for entities that no longer exist, including resources whose names could collide with future entity ids.

[ADVISORY] In getClientsWithPermission, the 'all-clients' type resource is created with type CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, so findByType includes it and hasGrantedPermission adds its resource name (the literal type string 'Clients', not a client id) to the returned granted set whenever the caller holds an all-clients permission. Callers of getClientsWithPermission (e.g. client listing filtering) receive a bogus entry 'Clients' mixed in with real client UUIDs; any downstream lookup by that value fails or must special-case it, and the filter silently leaks the all-clients grant as if it were a client.

[ADVISORY] The private method getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken) is dead code — nothing in this class calls it. Dead code referencing ClientModelIdentity/DefaultEvaluationContext survives review cycles; the next maintainer cannot tell whether token-exchange evaluation is intentionally omitted or accidentally disconnected, and any future caller wiring it in will bypass the UnsupportedOperationException guard pattern used by the sibling exchange methods.

[ADVISORY] canMapClientScopeRoles and the new MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE scope are implemented in this diff but no test in the diff ever grants or exercises MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE. Checked test files in the diff: PermissionClientTest.java (grants only MANAGE, CONFIGURE, VIEW, MAP_ROLES, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE), UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java, PermissionRESTTest.java, AbstractPermissionTest.java — none reference MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE. A regression in canMapClientScopeRoles (e.g., wiring the wrong scope constant) would pass CI silently; the new scope ships unverified.

[ADVISORY] resolveClient's fallback branch (getClientByClientId when getClientById returns null) is never exercised by any test in the diff. Checked PermissionClientTest.java, UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java, PermissionRESTTest.java — every client permission is created with myclient.getId() (a UUID), so the client-id fallback path (and the case where neither lookup resolves, returning null and producing the resource-name-null behavior) is untested; a regression there breaks creating permissions by clientId, which is the documented ergonomics for Users (username) and would silently diverge.

[ADVISORY] The new Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) gate around all three removal-event handlers is a changed branch with no test in the diff triggering either branch of the listener. When the feature is disabled, client/role/group deletion no longer disables permissions (resource cleanup silently skipped, orphaned permission resources accumulate); no test in the diff runs the listener with the feature off or on, so a typo reverting the gate or dropping a branch passes CI. Checked PermissionClientTest.java, UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java, PermissionRESTTest.java — none exercise ProviderEvent removal paths.

[ADVISORY] testViewAllClients 'can't create a new client' negative check sends create(null), which does not exercise the permission evaluator on a real create request. A null body is rejected by resource-layer validation/serialization before (or instead of) the authorization check, so the assertion Status.FORBIDDEN verifies that null bodies are refused, not that a VIEW-only admin cannot create a client; a regression granting create access to VIEW-only admins would not be caught by this assertion. The equivalent testManageAllClients pre-check uses a valid ClientRepresentation and is correct.

[ADVISORY] testConfigureOnlyOneClient asserts client-scope management boundaries (remove/add default scope forbidden under CONFIGURE) but never grants MANAGE to verify the allowed counterpart branch of the same endpoints. Only the negative half of the CONFIGURE-vs-MANAGE split for default/optional client-scope endpoints is asserted; the diff's requireManageClientScopes/canManageClientScopes V2 branch (MANAGE scope on the Clients type) is never positively exercised for client scopes in any test in this diff (checked PermissionClientTest.java, UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java, PermissionRESTTest.java), so a regression that denies scope management even with MANAGE passes CI.

[ADVISORY] Wrapping the ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent/RoleRemovedEvent cleanup handlers inside Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) means client, group, and role deletion no longer removes their associated permission resources/scopes when the feature is disabled, whereas the previous code ran this cleanup unconditionally. Realms that enabled fine-grained authz, created permission resources, then had the feature disabled at runtime accumulate orphaned authorization resources referencing deleted clients/roles/groups; if the feature is re-enabled later, stale resources for non-existent entities are resurrected and can silently grant or deny permissions during evaluation.

[BUG] All V2-only inherited operations (canExchangeTo, exchangeToPermission, mapRolesPermission, managePermission, configurePermission, viewPermission, isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, resource, getPermissions) throw raw UnsupportedOperationException, which surfaces as a 500 instead of the 4xx the admin API contract promises when any caller (e.g. legacy permissions endpoints or admin console code paths) reaches them while the V2 evaluator is active. A client-permission management request that previously returned 4xx/200 in the V1 path now returns a server error, and the Java stack of UnsupportedOperationException is logged as an unexpected server failure for what is an unsupported-feature condition.

[BUG] The ProviderEventListener now skips all remove-event cleanup (setPermissionsEnabled(false) for roles, clients, groups) whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is not enabled, so permission resources/policies created while the feature was enabled are silently left behind when the feature is later disabled and entities are deleted. Orphaned authorization resources and policies accumulate in the store with no cleanup path; re-enabling the feature later surfaces stale permission artifacts for deleted entities, and the failure is invisible because the event handler silently does nothing.

[ADVISORY] The private getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken) method is never referenced anywhere in this class (canExchangeTo, the only plausible caller, throws UnsupportedOperationException), so it is dead code. Future readers must reason about a ClientModelIdentity/DefaultEvaluationContext construction path that cannot execute; the next change to token-exchange support may resurrect a stale, untested context builder instead of writing one against current behavior.

[ADVISORY] The two hasPermission overloads (client-scoped and all-clients) duplicate the identical isAdminSameRealm guard, realmResourceServer null check, evaluatePermission call, and scope-matching loop, differing only in resource lookup. Any future fix to the permission-evaluation sequence (e.g. adding server null handling in one copy — note hasGrantedPermission at line 282 also re-duplicates the loop with no null guard) must be applied in three places, and drift between them changes grant semantics inconsistently across list vs. single-client checks.

[ADVISORY] In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no per-client resource exists the code falls back to the all-clients resource and checks only whether ANY policy is attached to it before evaluating, which conflates 'a policy exists for the all-clients resource' with 'the caller is granted the requested scope'. If the all-clients resource carries policies granting only a different scope (e.g. VIEW) while the caller requests MANAGE, the evaluation still runs and the result depends entirely on policy evaluation side effects rather than an early, clear denial — a debugger tracing a denied MANAGE request sees evaluation against a resource that was never meant to represent this client, misdirecting debugging of false-allow/false-deny reports.

[ADVISORY] resolveClient silently maps any unrecognized identifier through two lookups (internal id, then clientId) and returns null with no logging, so getOrCreateResource receives a null name for mistyped client ids and the caller's outcome depends entirely on the unseen null branch. An operator creating a permission against a deleted or cross-realm client gets whatever generic error the name==null branch produces (or, if that branch is permissive, a permission bound to a name that never resolves), with no log record identifying which id failed resolution — repeated silent no-op permission grants are plausible on the retry path.

goldens.comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

Since there is no import hunk shown, we cannot verify from the diff whether `org.keycloak.common.Profile` was already imported (or otherwise available), so the claim that it "does not compile as written" is not strictly verifiable from the provided diff alone.

adjudication.rationale: In `AdminPermissions.registerListener`, when `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` is enabled it handles `ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent` by calling `management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getClient(), false)`. This diff adds `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` returning `ClientPermissionsV2`, and `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled(...)` is implemented as `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE scope is added to the schema and wired into canMapClientScopeRoles(), but no test in this diff exercises it — PermissionClientTest covers MAP_ROLES and MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE (testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient) and never the client-scope map-roles path. adjudication.rationale: The diff adds the new scope constant AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE, registers it under the new CLIENTS resource type, and wires it into ClientPermissionsV2.canMapClientScopeRoles(ClientModel) via hasPermission(client, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE). However, the added/modified tests in this diff (notably PermissionClientTest.testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient) only exercise MAP_ROLES and MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE and never grant or assert behavior for MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE. So a typo or evaluation bug specific to MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE would not be caught by these tests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The private method getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken) is dead code — nothing in the class invokes it because canExchangeTo and all exchange-related methods throw UnsupportedOperationException. Next change to token-exchange support in V2 must first determine whether this half-attached evaluation context (with its kc.client.id attribute) is the intended entry point or a leftover from a reverted approach; until then it rots invisibly and misleads readers into thinking token-exchange evaluation is partially wired.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `ClientPermissionsV2` class, the private method `getEvaluationContext(ClientModel authorizedClient, AccessToken token)` is defined but never invoked anywhere in the class. At the same time, all token-exchange related entry points (`canExchangeTo`, `exchangeToPermission`, and other exchange/map permission methods) unconditionally throw `UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`, so there is no visible execution path in this diff that would use that evaluation context or its custom `kc.client.id` attribute. This is diff-grounded dead code that can mislead readers about partially implemented token-exchange support.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] In getClientsWithPermission, `granted.add(resource.getName())` returns the resource name, which getOrCreateResource sets via resolveClient() to `client.getId()` (the internal UUID), while callers consuming this set to filter the clients list match against client representations whose `id` field is the internal id but whose user-facing identifier is `clientId`. If any caller filters by clientId rather than internal id (the natural mistake given the method name and the admin REST surface), the filtered list silently drops every granted client; the existing tests only assert non-empty/empty results, not the identity of the returned strings, so a name-vs-id mismatch passes the suite.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that client resources are named with the internal UUID: AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource() uses resolveClient(), which returns client.getId(), and ClientPermissionsV2.getClientsWithPermission() collects resource.getName() into the returned Set. Whether this is a defect depends on how callers interpret the returned strings (internal id vs clientId), but the diff does not show any consumer. However, the method name/returned value contract is ambiguous and the added tests only check empty/non-empty or list sizes, not that the returned identifiers are the expected form, so a future/other caller could easily misuse it.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new javadoc on requireView() (and requireListClientScopes()-adjacent void require methods) states 'Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}' for methods declared `void` that throw ForbiddenException — the contract is documented as a boolean query when it is an enforcement call. Call-site authors reading the interface contract treat requireView() as a check they can call speculatively, and get an HTTP-500-style ForbiddenException propagated instead of a false return, producing wrong exception handling in new admin endpoints.

adjudication.rationale: In `ClientPermissionEvaluator`, several new Javadocs describe `require*` methods (which are declared `void`) using boolean-return wording like “Returns {@code true} if …” (e.g., the comment immediately above `void requireView();` says “Returns {@code true} if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}.”). This is a real, diff-grounded contract/documentation problem that can mislead API users, but the diff does not show any actual behavioral change or new call-sites relying on the incorrect documentation, so it’s not a verifiable runtime bug introduced by this PR.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The PR wraps the pre-existing role/client/group removal cleanup logic in Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ), changing behavior that is not traceable to the stated intent of adding a Clients resource type. In deployments where the feature was previously compiled-in but this listener previously ran unconditionally, disabling the feature now silently skips setPermissionsEnabled(false) cleanup on role/client/group deletion, leaving orphaned permission resources in the database that the old code removed — a data-hygiene regression unrelated to adding the Clients resource type.

adjudication.rationale: In services/.../AdminPermissions.java, the deletion-event cleanup (calling management(...).roles()/clients()/groups().setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)) previously ran unconditionally, but is now guarded by Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ). This is a verifiable behavior change: when the feature flag is off, the listener will no longer perform cleanup on RoleRemoved/ClientRemoved/GroupRemoved events. Whether this is a true defect (e.g., leaving orphaned authz artifacts) depends on intended semantics when the feature is disabled, which the diff alone does not establish.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, but the AdminPermissions event listener added in this same diff calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false) on every ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled. With the V2 permissions path active, deleting any client throws UnsupportedOperationException during event handling, turning client deletion (a previously working operation, now also exercised by testManageAllClients' delete step) into a 500 error instead of completing the removal.

adjudication.rationale: The diff makes the admin permissions event listener call `management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getClient(), false)` on every `ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent` when `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` is enabled (see `AdminPermissions.java`). In the same diff, the V2 implementation `ClientPermissionsV2` overrides `setPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel, boolean)` to unconditionally throw `UnsupportedOperationException` (see `ClientPermissionsV2.java`). Additionally, `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` is newly overridden to return `ClientPermissionsV2`, meaning that if `management(...)` resolves to the V2 permissions root, client removal will trigger this exception during event handling, likely turning client deletion into a server error.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getEvaluationContext and the TOKEN_EXCHANGE static import are dead code in this diff — getEvaluationContext is never called (all token-exchange methods throw UnsupportedOperationException) and TOKEN_EXCHANGE is referenced nowhere in the class body. Future readers must reason about an evaluation-context path that cannot execute; the next change to token-exchange support risks building on a code path that has never been exercised, and the unused import fails strict import checks.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `ClientPermissionsV2` class, there is a static import `import static org.keycloak.services.resources.admin.permissions.AdminPermissionManagement.TOKEN_EXCHANGE;` that is not referenced anywhere in the class body. Also, the private method `getEvaluationContext(ClientModel authorizedClient, AccessToken token)` is defined but never called within this diff; all token-exchange related overrides (`canExchangeTo`, `exchangeToPermission`, etc.) immediately throw `UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`, so there is no visible execution path that would use this evaluation context. This is a concrete maintainability/cleanup issue and may trip unused-import tooling, but it is not a directly verifiable runtime defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE scope is added to the schema and canMapClientScopeRoles is implemented, but no test in this diff exercises it and no admin REST path in the diff is shown enforcing it, unlike MAP_ROLES and MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE which testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient covers. A regression in the map-roles-client-scope evaluation (e.g., a wrong scope constant or a mis-wired caller) ships undetected; operators granting the scope get behavior that is never validated, breaking the parity-with-V1 invariant the other five scopes' tests establish.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds the new scope constant `MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE` to `AdminPermissionsSchema` and implements `ClientPermissionsV2.canMapClientScopeRoles()` by checking `hasPermission(client, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE)`. However, the new/updated tests in this diff (notably `PermissionClientTest.testMapRolesAndCompositesOnlyOneClient`) only exercise `MAP_ROLES` and `MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE` (and `CONFIGURE`), and do not create or validate behavior gated by `MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE`. Also, within this diff there is no shown REST enforcement callsite that specifically requires `canMapClientScopeRoles`/`MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE`, so a wiring/constant regression for this scope would not be covered by the added tests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Twelve overridden methods throw UnsupportedOperationException rather than the interface being narrowed or the V2-only surface being split out, so any caller not updated in this diff that touches exchangeTo, resource(), getPermissions, etc. fails at runtime instead of at compile time. Any existing or out-of-tree caller of ClientPermissionEvaluator's per-client policy-management methods (e.g., the admin PermissionsResource endpoints) that reaches the V2 implementation gets a raw UnsupportedOperationException/500 instead of a documented 4xx; the compiler can no longer flag new call sites added later.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `ClientPermissionsV2` which overrides a number of existing `ClientPermissions` operations by throwing `UnsupportedOperationException` (e.g., `setPermissionsEnabled`, `resource`, `getPermissions`, and several `*Permission(...)` methods). In the same diff, `AdminPermissions.registerListener` still calls `management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getClient(), false)` on `ClientRemovedEvent` (now gated only by `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ`). If `management(...).clients()` resolves to the new V2 implementation (as implied by `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` returning `ClientPermissionsV2`), that event path will now throw at runtime instead of performing cleanup, yielding an unhandled exception.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Under the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature flag the removal listener calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(...), which in the V2 implementation (ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled) throws UnsupportedOperationException, so deleting a client while the feature is enabled fails instead of cleaning up permissions. Client deletion (and role/group deletion via the same guarded block) raises UnsupportedOperationException during the removal event, breaking a core admin operation for realms that enabled the feature; if the flag gates V1 management() the entire block now dead-codes for realms without the feature, leaving orphaned permission resources on removal.

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, the removal listener in `AdminPermissions.registerListener` is now executed only when `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` and, on `ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent`, it calls `management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getClient(), false)`. The newly added `ClientPermissionsV2` explicitly overrides `setPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel client, boolean enable)` to `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`. If the feature-enabled path wires `management(...).clients()` to the V2 implementation (consistent with the new `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` returning `ClientPermissionsV2`), the listener will throw during client removal, breaking deletion/cleanup behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] resolveClient accepts either the internal UUID or the clientId and returns the canonical id, but the resource is created/stored named by whatever string the permission-creation path passed, while ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission looks the resource up by client.getId() — the two paths can disagree on the resource name for the same client. A permission created referencing the client by clientId produces a resource named by the clientId; a subsequent evaluation for that client does findByName(server, client.getId()) and misses it, so the granted permission silently does not apply (deny instead of allow), or two resources accumulate for one client and list/getClientsWithPermission reports inconsistent results depending on which name was used.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource now handles CLIENTS by calling resolveClient(session, id), and resolveClient returns the canonical internal client UUID (client.getId()) regardless of whether the caller passed an internal id or a clientId (it tries getClientById first, then getClientByClientId, and returns client.getId()). Therefore, a permission created referencing a client by clientId would still result in a resource named by the internal UUID, matching ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission which looks up by client.getId(). The described mismatch (resource stored under clientId string but evaluated via UUID) is not supported by this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] getClientsWithPermission iterates every resource of type Clients and calls hasGrantedPermission, which invokes root.evaluatePermission (a full policy evaluation, loading policies from the store) once per client resource — an N+1 evaluation loop over a collection that scales with the number of clients in the realm. On any admin client-listing path that filters by granted permission, a realm with thousands of clients performs thousands of full permission evaluations per request, turning the list endpoint into an O(n) policy-evaluation workload with no pagination or batching; large realms see severe latency and DB load on a hot admin path.

adjudication.rationale: In `ClientPermissionsV2#getClientsWithPermission`, the code calls `resourceStore.findByType(..., resource -> { if (hasGrantedPermission(resource, scope)) ... })`, and `hasGrantedPermission` invokes `root.evaluatePermission(new ResourcePermission(...))` for each resource. This is an O(n) per-request loop of full permission evaluations over all `Clients`-typed resources, with no batching/pagination in this method. The diff does not show the call sites to confirm it is on a hot client-listing path, so the “severe latency on admin list endpoint” impact is plausible but not verifiable from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getEvaluationContext (and the TOKEN_EXCHANGE static import it supports) is dead code — nothing in the class calls it, and canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException. The next maintainer must reason about and possibly maintain an evaluation-context path that is never exercised; when token-exchange support is added it will likely be copied from this stale skeleton rather than the real V1 behavior.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `ClientPermissionsV2` class, the private method `getEvaluationContext(ClientModel authorizedClient, AccessToken token)` is not referenced anywhere in the file, and the static import `import static org.keycloak.services.resources.admin.permissions.AdminPermissionManagement.TOKEN_EXCHANGE;` is also unused. Additionally, token-exchange related overrides (`canExchangeTo`, `exchangeToPermission`) immediately throw `UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`, so there is no execution path in this class that would exercise an evaluation-context-based token-exchange implementation. This is a concrete maintainability issue introduced by the diff (dead code/skeleton that could mislead future changes), but not a functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The evaluate-permissions-and-scan-for-scope loop is duplicated three times (hasPermission(ClientModel,String), hasPermission(String), hasGrantedPermission), differing only in how the Resource is obtained. When the scope-matching logic changes (e.g. to support scope collections or wildcard grants), three copies must be updated in lockstep; missing one yields evaluator methods that disagree on whether a scope is granted — a silent authorization inconsistency.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `ClientPermissionsV2` class, the scope-evaluation logic is indeed duplicated in three places: `hasPermission(ClientModel,String)` (loops over `root.evaluatePermission(...)` results and matches `scope` against `permission.getScopes()`), `hasPermission(String)` (same loop, different resource lookup), and `hasGrantedPermission(Resource,String)` (same loop again). The only meaningful difference is how the `Resource` is obtained before evaluation. This is not a current functional defect, but it is a concrete maintainability/consistency risk introduced by the diff: future changes to scope matching would need to be applied in three methods to avoid divergent authorization decisions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] canMapRoles/canMapCompositeRoles/canMapClientScopeRoles in V2 drop the previous base-class fallback entirely and rely solely on hasPermission, while canConfigure and canManage keep the admin-role short-circuit — an inconsistent ownership of 'who can map roles' between the role-based and FGAP paths. An admin holding MANAGE_CLIENTS but no explicit map-roles permission can manage the client yet cannot map its roles in V2, a behavior change vs V1 that any caller (or test) assuming role-superset semantics will hit as an unexpected ForbiddenException.

adjudication.rationale: In `ClientPermissionsV2`, `canMapRoles(...)`, `canMapCompositeRoles(...)`, and `canMapClientScopeRoles(...)` are overridden to *only* return `hasPermission(client, ...)` (no `root.hasOneAdminRole(...)` short-circuit and no `super.*` fallback), unlike `canManage(ClientModel)` / `canConfigure(ClientModel)` / `canManageClientScopes()` which explicitly honor `AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS` (e.g., `if (root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS)) return true;`). This creates a verifiable inconsistency: a caller with the role-based `MANAGE_CLIENTS` capability can pass `canManage(client)` but still fail the map-roles checks in V2, leading to unexpected `ForbiddenException` for role-mapping operations when FGAP V2 is enabled.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getPermissionsResource, getScopePermissionsResource, and createPermission were converted from instance methods to static methods taking ManagedClient, a breaking signature change to a shared test base class whose out-of-tree subclasses call the no-arg forms. Any external test module extending AbstractPermissionTest and calling getPermissionsResource() with no arguments no longer compiles after upgrading, with no deprecation window.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `AbstractPermissionTest` changing `getPermissionsResource()`, `getScopePermissionsResource()`, and `createPermission(...)` from instance/no-arg helpers to `static` methods that require a `ManagedClient` parameter (e.g., `protected static PermissionsResource getPermissionsResource(ManagedClient client)` and `protected static void createPermission(ManagedClient client, ...)`). This is a signature/API change to a shared test base class; any external/out-of-tree subclasses that previously called the no-arg instance methods would no longer compile. This is a compatibility concern rather than an in-repo runtime correctness bug, and the change is directly verifiable in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The RoleRemovedEvent/ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent cleanup handlers were silently re-gated behind Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ), changing previously unconditional cleanup behavior as an incidental side effect of a PR whose stated intent is only to add a Clients resource type. When the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature is disabled (the pre-existing V1 fine-grained permissions deployments), deleting a role, client, or group no longer calls setPermissionsEnabled(..., false), leaving orphaned permission resources and policies in the database that reappear/grant stale access if the feature is later re-enabled.

adjudication.rationale: The diff in AdminPermissions.registerListener wraps previously unconditional cleanup on RoleRemovedEvent/ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent inside `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)) { ... }`. That is a verifiable behavior change: when the feature is disabled, the listener now performs no `setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)` calls on deletions, whereas before it did. This can plausibly leave authz artifacts (permissions/resources/policies) uncleared in those deployments, i.e., orphaned data that would have been cleaned up previously.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, but the ClientRemovedEvent handler in AdminPermissions.management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false) is the code path that must run on every client deletion, so V2 realms throw during client removal. With the feature enabled and MgmtPermissionsV2 in use, deleting any client propagates an UnsupportedOperationException out of the event listener instead of disabling its permissions, failing the client-deletion flow that the intent of the PR (managing client permissions) presupposes works.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel, boolean)` throws `UnsupportedOperationException` (new file `ClientPermissionsV2.java`). The event listener in `AdminPermissions.registerListener` calls `management(session, realm).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getClient(), false)` on every `ClientRemovedEvent`, and this call is now guarded by `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)`. The diff also shows `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` is overridden to return `ClientPermissionsV2`. Therefore, in the V2 permissions implementation, a client deletion event can invoke `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled(...)` and throw, potentially breaking the client-deletion flow.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The ClientRemovedEvent/RoleRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent handlers call clients().setPermissionsEnabled(...) which now throws UnsupportedOperationException when the V2 ClientPermissions implementation is active under the enabled ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ feature, so deleting a client/role/group in a V2 realm blows up inside event processing. When the feature is enabled and the V2 permission implementation is in use, entity deletion triggers UnsupportedOperationException from the event listener (instead of the previous no-op/cleanup), failing or polluting the delete path for clients, roles, and groups.

adjudication.rationale: In `AdminPermissions.registerListener`, when `Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` is enabled, the event listener now calls `management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getClient(), false)` for `ClientRemovedEvent` (and similarly for roles/groups). This diff introduces `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` returning `ClientPermissionsV2`, where `setPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel, boolean)` is overridden to `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`. Therefore, if the V2 permissions implementation is active while the feature is enabled, deleting a client will trigger an `UnsupportedOperationException` during event processing, breaking the delete flow/cleanup path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Wrapping the removal-event cleanup in Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) means authorization resource cleanup for deleted clients/roles/groups no longer runs when the feature is off, leaving orphaned permission resources in the database. An operator who disables the feature after having created fine-grained permissions accumulates stale resources; re-enabling the feature later resurrects permission entries for entities that no longer exist, including resources whose names could collide with future entity ids.

adjudication.rationale: In AdminPermissions.registerListener, the PR wraps all removal-event handling (RoleRemovedEvent, ClientRemovedEvent, GroupRemovedEvent) inside `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))` (see modified `onEvent`). Previously, `setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)` was invoked unconditionally on these deletion events. With this change, if the feature is disabled at deletion time, the cleanup/disable path will not run, so any authorization/permission artifacts tied to the deleted entity will not be cleared by this listener. The diff directly shows this behavioral regression in cleanup execution when the feature is off.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] In getClientsWithPermission, the 'all-clients' type resource is created with type CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, so findByType includes it and hasGrantedPermission adds its resource name (the literal type string 'Clients', not a client id) to the returned granted set whenever the caller holds an all-clients permission. Callers of getClientsWithPermission (e.g. client listing filtering) receive a bogus entry 'Clients' mixed in with real client UUIDs; any downstream lookup by that value fails or must special-case it, and the filter silently leaks the all-clients grant as if it were a client.
matched_golden_ids: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: The candidate flags that getClientsWithPermission iterates type-level CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE resources (including the all-clients resource) and returns the resource name ('Clients' / type string) rather than actual per-client IDs, producing a bogus entry that downstream code treats as a client ID and fails. This is the same underlying issue described in the golden comment (wrong resource type/name leading to null/incorrect client lookup).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The private method getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken) is dead code — nothing in this class calls it. Dead code referencing ClientModelIdentity/DefaultEvaluationContext survives review cycles; the next maintainer cannot tell whether token-exchange evaluation is intentionally omitted or accidentally disconnected, and any future caller wiring it in will bypass the UnsupportedOperationException guard pattern used by the sibling exchange methods.

adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue point out that the private method getEvaluationContext(...) in ClientPermissionsV2 is defined but never called (dead/unused code) and should be removed or addressed.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] canMapClientScopeRoles and the new MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE scope are implemented in this diff but no test in the diff ever grants or exercises MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE. Checked test files in the diff: PermissionClientTest.java (grants only MANAGE, CONFIGURE, VIEW, MAP_ROLES, MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE), UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java, PermissionRESTTest.java, AbstractPermissionTest.java — none reference MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE. A regression in canMapClientScopeRoles (e.g., wiring the wrong scope constant) would pass CI silently; the new scope ships unverified.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new scope constant `MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE` in `AdminPermissionsSchema` and wires it into `ClientPermissionsV2.canMapClientScopeRoles(ClientModel)` via `hasPermission(client, AdminPermissionsSchema.MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE)`. However, the added/modified tests in the diff never grant or assert behavior tied to `MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE` (e.g., `PermissionClientTest` only uses/grants `MANAGE`, `CONFIGURE`, `VIEW`, `MAP_ROLES`, `MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE`). As a result, a regression such as using the wrong scope constant in `canMapClientScopeRoles` would not be caught by CI based on the shown tests.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] resolveClient's fallback branch (getClientByClientId when getClientById returns null) is never exercised by any test in the diff. Checked PermissionClientTest.java, UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java, PermissionRESTTest.java — every client permission is created with myclient.getId() (a UUID), so the client-id fallback path (and the case where neither lookup resolves, returning null and producing the resource-name-null behavior) is untested; a regression there breaks creating permissions by clientId, which is the documented ergonomics for Users (username) and would silently diverge.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveClient(), which first calls session.clients().getClientById(realm, id) and then falls back to getClientByClientId(realm, id) if null. In the added/modified tests (e.g., PermissionClientTest.testManageOnlyOneClient/testConfigureOnlyOneClient and others), permissions for a specific client are created using myclient.getId() (UUID) as the resource identifier (createPermission(..., myclient.getId(), clientsType, ...)), so the getClientByClientId fallback branch is not exercised. The diff also doesn’t add a test covering the case where both lookups fail (name == null path leading to bad request behavior). This is a concrete missing-test gap for newly introduced nontrivial resolution logic, not a directly verifiable functional defect in the code itself.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) gate around all three removal-event handlers is a changed branch with no test in the diff triggering either branch of the listener. When the feature is disabled, client/role/group deletion no longer disables permissions (resource cleanup silently skipped, orphaned permission resources accumulate); no test in the diff runs the listener with the feature off or on, so a typo reverting the gate or dropping a branch passes CI. Checked PermissionClientTest.java, UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java, PermissionRESTTest.java — none exercise ProviderEvent removal paths.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes AdminPermissions.registerListener() so that *all* three removal-event handlers (RoleRemovedEvent/ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent) run only when Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) is true. That is a non-trivial behavioral gate added around cleanup logic (setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)). The added/modified tests in this diff (e.g., PermissionClientTest, UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest, PermissionRESTTest) create/evaluate permissions but do not exercise ProviderEventManager listener behavior on role/client/group removal with the feature enabled/disabled. So the concern about missing test coverage for the new feature-flag branch is grounded in the shown changes. Whether this is an actual bug (or intended to avoid cleanup when the feature is off) cannot be proven from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] testViewAllClients 'can't create a new client' negative check sends create(null), which does not exercise the permission evaluator on a real create request. A null body is rejected by resource-layer validation/serialization before (or instead of) the authorization check, so the assertion Status.FORBIDDEN verifies that null bodies are refused, not that a VIEW-only admin cannot create a client; a regression granting create access to VIEW-only admins would not be caught by this assertion. The equivalent testManageAllClients pre-check uses a valid ClientRepresentation and is correct.

adjudication.rationale: In `PermissionClientTest.testViewAllClients`, the negative check for “can't create a new client” calls `realmAdminClient.realm(realm.getName()).clients().create(null)` and asserts `Status.FORBIDDEN`. The diff shows the request body is `null`, unlike `testManageAllClients` which uses a valid `ClientRepresentation`. Using a null body can fail due to request/serialization/validation before authorization is evaluated, so this assertion may not actually verify that VIEW-only permissions cannot create clients, weakening the test coverage for the newly added client permission logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] testConfigureOnlyOneClient asserts client-scope management boundaries (remove/add default scope forbidden under CONFIGURE) but never grants MANAGE to verify the allowed counterpart branch of the same endpoints. Only the negative half of the CONFIGURE-vs-MANAGE split for default/optional client-scope endpoints is asserted; the diff's requireManageClientScopes/canManageClientScopes V2 branch (MANAGE scope on the Clients type) is never positively exercised for client scopes in any test in this diff (checked PermissionClientTest.java, UserResourceTypeEvaluationTest.java, PermissionRESTTest.java), so a regression that denies scope management even with MANAGE passes CI.

adjudication.rationale: The diff *does* positively exercise the MANAGE branch for client-scope endpoints. In `PermissionClientTest#testManageOnlyOneClient`, it grants a client-specific permission with `Set.of(MANAGE)` via `createPermission(client, myclient.getId(), clientsType, Set.of(MANAGE), ...)`, and then successfully calls `clientResource.removeDefaultClientScope(...)` and `clientResource.addOptionalClientScope(...)`. This directly covers the allowed counterpart to the CONFIGURE-only negative assertions in `testConfigureOnlyOneClient` and would fail if a regression denied scope management even with MANAGE.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Wrapping the ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent/RoleRemovedEvent cleanup handlers inside Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ) means client, group, and role deletion no longer removes their associated permission resources/scopes when the feature is disabled, whereas the previous code ran this cleanup unconditionally. Realms that enabled fine-grained authz, created permission resources, then had the feature disabled at runtime accumulate orphaned authorization resources referencing deleted clients/roles/groups; if the feature is re-enabled later, stale resources for non-existent entities are resurrected and can silently grant or deny permissions during evaluation.

adjudication.rationale: In services/.../AdminPermissions.java, the PR adds an outer guard `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)) { ... }` around all three removal handlers (RoleRemovedEvent/ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent). Previously, those events always triggered `setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)` cleanup. With this diff, when the feature flag is disabled, deletions will no longer invoke this cleanup, so any previously-created fine-grained authz resources/policies tied to deleted roles/clients/groups can remain orphaned. This is a concrete behavioral regression introduced by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] All V2-only inherited operations (canExchangeTo, exchangeToPermission, mapRolesPermission, managePermission, configurePermission, viewPermission, isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, resource, getPermissions) throw raw UnsupportedOperationException, which surfaces as a 500 instead of the 4xx the admin API contract promises when any caller (e.g. legacy permissions endpoints or admin console code paths) reaches them while the V2 evaluator is active. A client-permission management request that previously returned 4xx/200 in the V1 path now returns a server error, and the Java stack of UnsupportedOperationException is logged as an unexpected server failure for what is an unsupported-feature condition.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does show that many overridden methods in `ClientPermissionsV2` (`canExchangeTo`, `exchangeToPermission`, `mapRolesPermission`, `mapRolesClientScopePermission`, `mapRolesCompositePermission`, `managePermission`, `configurePermission`, `viewPermission`, `isPermissionsEnabled`, `setPermissionsEnabled`, `resource`, `getPermissions`) unconditionally `throw new UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`. Since `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` is changed to return `new ClientPermissionsV2(...)`, these exceptions could propagate if any V2 code path calls those methods. However, the diff does not prove that any REST/admin-console/legacy endpoint will invoke these methods while V2 is active, nor that the framework will necessarily translate `UnsupportedOperationException` into a 500 vs. a mapped 4xx. So the finding’s specific runtime impact (500 regression) isn’t directly verifiable from the diff, but the risk/contract concern is real and diff-grounded.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The ProviderEventListener now skips all remove-event cleanup (setPermissionsEnabled(false) for roles, clients, groups) whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is not enabled, so permission resources/policies created while the feature was enabled are silently left behind when the feature is later disabled and entities are deleted. Orphaned authorization resources and policies accumulate in the store with no cleanup path; re-enabling the feature later surfaces stale permission artifacts for deleted entities, and the failure is invisible because the event handler silently does nothing.

adjudication.rationale: In `AdminPermissions.registerListener`, the diff adds an outer guard `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)) { ... }` around *all* remove-event handling. Previously, `RoleRemovedEvent`, `ClientRemovedEvent`, and `GroupRemovedEvent` always triggered `setPermissionsEnabled(..., false)` cleanup; now, when the feature is disabled, the listener performs no cleanup at all. This directly enables the described scenario where authorization artifacts created while the feature was enabled can be left orphaned if entities are removed after the feature is turned off, since the only shown cleanup path is now skipped.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The private getEvaluationContext(ClientModel, AccessToken) method is never referenced anywhere in this class (canExchangeTo, the only plausible caller, throws UnsupportedOperationException), so it is dead code. Future readers must reason about a ClientModelIdentity/DefaultEvaluationContext construction path that cannot execute; the next change to token-exchange support may resurrect a stale, untested context builder instead of writing one against current behavior.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `ClientPermissionsV2` class, the private method `getEvaluationContext(ClientModel authorizedClient, AccessToken token)` is defined but never called anywhere in that class. The only methods that look like they might need an evaluation context (`canExchangeTo`, `exchangeToPermission`, etc.) all currently throw `UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`, so there is no execution path in this diff that would reference `getEvaluationContext`. This is real dead code introduced by the diff and can mislead future maintainers.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The two hasPermission overloads (client-scoped and all-clients) duplicate the identical isAdminSameRealm guard, realmResourceServer null check, evaluatePermission call, and scope-matching loop, differing only in resource lookup. Any future fix to the permission-evaluation sequence (e.g. adding server null handling in one copy — note hasGrantedPermission at line 282 also re-duplicates the loop with no null guard) must be applied in three places, and drift between them changes grant semantics inconsistently across list vs. single-client checks.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `ClientPermissionsV2` the permission-evaluation logic is indeed duplicated across `hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope)`, `hasPermission(String scope)`, and `hasGrantedPermission(Resource resource, String scope)`: each contains the same `root.isAdminSameRealm()` guard (first two), `realmResourceServer()` retrieval (all three), `root.evaluatePermission(new ResourcePermission(...))` call, and nested loop to match scopes. The only substantive difference between the two `hasPermission` overloads is how the `Resource` is looked up. This creates a real maintainability/drift risk grounded in the diff (and `hasGrantedPermission` also reimplements the scope-matching loop and re-fetches the server without its own null guard).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no per-client resource exists the code falls back to the all-clients resource and checks only whether ANY policy is attached to it before evaluating, which conflates 'a policy exists for the all-clients resource' with 'the caller is granted the requested scope'. If the all-clients resource carries policies granting only a different scope (e.g. VIEW) while the caller requests MANAGE, the evaluation still runs and the result depends entirely on policy evaluation side effects rather than an early, clear denial — a debugger tracing a denied MANAGE request sees evaluation against a resource that was never meant to represent this client, misdirecting debugging of false-allow/false-deny reports.

adjudication.rationale: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission(ClientModel,String), the fallback to the all-clients resource only occurs when no per-client resource exists, and it does not treat “any policy exists” as “scope granted”. After the non-empty policy check, it evaluates permissions and explicitly returns true only if the evaluated Permission contains the requested scope (it iterates permission.getScopes() and matches against the requested scope). If the all-clients policies grant only VIEW and the request is MANAGE, the method returns false. The finding’s claim of conflation/false-allow due to the mere existence check is not supported by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] resolveClient silently maps any unrecognized identifier through two lookups (internal id, then clientId) and returns null with no logging, so getOrCreateResource receives a null name for mistyped client ids and the caller's outcome depends entirely on the unseen null branch. An operator creating a permission against a deleted or cross-realm client gets whatever generic error the name==null branch produces (or, if that branch is permissive, a permission bound to a name that never resolves), with no log record identifying which id failed resolution — repeated silent no-op permission grants are plausible on the retry path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `resolveClient(KeycloakSession, String)` which tries `getClientById(realm, id)` then `getClientByClientId(realm, id)` and returns `null` if neither exists, with no logging. `getOrCreateResource(...)` was updated to call this for `CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE`, and then relies on the existing `if (name == null) { ... }` branch (not shown) for error/behavior. So the concern about silent resolution failure and lack of diagnostic information is diff-grounded; however, the claim about what the null-branch does (generic error vs permissive behavior / creating unusable permissions) cannot be verified from the provided diff snippet.
